topic_title: Why Are More Cities Rethinking Public Benches?

sources.title: Active Aging and Smart Public Parks
sources.authors_or_organization: Boavida, J., Ayanoglu, H., Pereira, C.V., Hernandez-Ramirez, R.
sources.fetched_extraction: This is a literature review examining smart public parks' role in promoting active aging for older adults. Methodology: literature analysis of 28 recent articles (2020-2023) categorized by objectives, environmental aspects, solutions, methodologies, and geographic locations; search of the Elicit database used the phrase 'Smart parks for elderly wellbeing.' Key finding on seating: 'older users prefer a higher number of benches in public parks as they are inclined toward relaxation' (citing Stanley et al. within the review). Well-maintained parks featuring 'seating, pleasant paths, toilets, cafes' encouraged older visitors (citing Veitch et al. within the review). The reviewers recommend combining qualitative techniques (focus groups, interviews, observations) with objective measurements of comfort and usability to get more precise data on bench design. Geographic distribution of the 28 reviewed studies: European studies dominated (n=15), followed by Chinese research (n=5). Limitation: this was not a systematic literature review, so the authors state it cannot be guaranteed that all relevant information was fully covered.

sources.title: "Benches become like porches": Built and social environment influences on older adults' experiences of mobility and well-being
sources.authors_or_organization: Ottoni, C.A., Sims-Gould, J., Winters, M., Heijnen, M., McKay, H.A.
sources.fetched_extraction: Qualitative study using one-on-one seated and walk-along interviews with adults aged 60+ living in three adjacent neighbourhoods in Vancouver, Canada, at two time points (n=28 in 2012; n=22 in 2014). Findings: benches positively contributed to older adults' mobility experiences by enhancing their use and enjoyment of green and blue (waterfront) spaces, serving as a literal mobility aid (a place to rest during a walk), and contributing to social cohesion and social capital -- the paper's title concept is that benches function like a 'porch,' a semi-public perch that supports casual social contact in the neighbourhood. NOTE: full text was not accessible (paywalled); these facts are drawn from the published abstract and third-party summaries of the study, not from directly reading the full paper.

sources.title: Hostile architecture (encyclopedia article aggregating multiple primary/secondary sources on bench removal and defensive design)
sources.authors_or_organization: Wikipedia contributors (aggregating cited academic and journalistic sources)
sources.fetched_extraction: Explains why cities modify or remove benches as 'hostile' or 'defensive' architecture: cited claim that cities have 'a vested interest in eliminating signs of homelessness from communal spaces, fearing it might discourage investment from wealthier individuals' (article citation [20]); in England, the practice is described as stemming from 'a desire by the government to combat an anti-social street scene, taking the form of begging and street drinking' (citation [21]). Documented general techniques (treat as CATEGORIES, not tied to a specific confirmed incident below): sloped benches that require the user to support themselves with their feet, 'ubiquitous at bus stops across the United Kingdom' (citation [34]); center armrests that prevent lying down across a bench (citation [35]); 'Camden benches,' concrete-block benches designed to discourage sleeping, skateboarding, and sticker-placement (citation [36]); outright removal, which Fredrik Edin (cited, [57]) describes as 'the most common form of exclusionary design, in which... benches used by the public are removed precisely because the public uses them.' Important limitation explicitly noted in the article: as of March 2020, 'no wide-scale empirical study has been conducted to measure the impact of hostile architecture on the wellbeing of homeless people or other targeted populations' (citation [63]). CORRECTION (2026-08-21, after production Writer Fact Check independently re-verified the named incidents below via live web search against contemporaneous reporting): the specific named incidents originally drawn from this Wikipedia article (Stockholm Central Station bench removal 'in 2015', Lulea iron-bar benches, and the Malmo tilted-bench date/intent) did NOT hold up to primary-source verification and must NOT be used as confirmed facts. See SRC-004 for the corrected, fact-checker-verified version of the Malmo and NYC examples, which ARE usable.

sources.title: Production Writer Fact Checker's independent live-web-search corroboration of specific named hostile-architecture incidents (Malmo tilted bench, NYC subway bench removal post)
sources.authors_or_organization: Findings surfaced by er003_v1_n3_01_articles_generate.py's production Fact Check gate (r3.run_fact_checker_with_gates), which has live web_search access; original reporting: Sveriges Radio, Aftonbladet
sources.journal_or_venue: sverigesradio.se; aftonbladet.se (as identified by the Fact Checker's own search)
sources.fetched_extraction: Malmo (Triangeln station, opened December 2010): a sloped/tilted bench design drew public complaints; the earliest confirmable contemporaneous report of a formal complaint to Sweden's Equality Ombudsman (DO) is dated 2011-03-04 (exact 2010 complaint date not independently confirmable). Importantly, a city official's 2011 explanation (per the Fact Checker's sourced summary) was that the bench had been ordered WITH a back and armrests specifically for accessibility reasons, but the seat that was delivered turned out to be more steeply tilted than intended, and the angle was subsequently corrected -- i.e., contemporaneous reporting describes this as an accessibility-design bench that came out more uncomfortable than planned and was then fixed, not a bench that was deliberately designed from the outset to be hostile. Some later commentators/researchers have nonetheless cited it as an example of sleep-deterrent design; the sources disagree on original intent. NYC Subway: a 2021 post from an NYC Transit official social-media account stated benches were being removed to stop homeless people from sleeping on them; the post was later deleted, and the MTA said it had been posted in error. This is a real, documented, dated public incident (a genuine example of the topic's social tension), but it should be presented as a since-retracted social-media statement, not as evidence of an adopted formal removal policy.
